tests: Recall at volume. Twelve labelled requirements in a long posting — the case where a model summarises instead of enumerating.
jd:
Staff Backend Engineer — Kestrel Payments (London / remote, UK)

Kestrel processes card payments for around 4,000 UK merchants. You would join the ledger team.

What you will do:
• Own the double-entry ledger service end to end
• Lead the migration off our legacy settlement batch
• Set the technical direction for the team's next two years

Requirements:
• 8+ years building backend services in production
• Deep expertise in Go, or strong systems experience and the appetite to learn it fast
• Postgres at scale: partitioning, query planning, and knowing when an index will not help
• Event-driven architecture using Kafka or an equivalent log
• A rigorous approach to idempotency and exactly-once semantics under retry
• Experience designing and evolving public APIs, including versioning and deprecation
• Track record of leading technical projects across more than one team
• Ability to mentor senior engineers, not only juniors
• Comfortable being the escalation point during a payments incident
• Written communication strong enough to carry a design across the company
• Understanding of PCI-DSS obligations as they apply to engineering
• Familiarity with double-entry bookkeeping concepts

Desirable:
• Prior work in payments, banking or another regulated financial environment
• Experience with gRPC

We interview with a take-home, a systems design session and two conversations.
notes: Twelve musts is the point: recall degrades as the list grows, and a model that returns six well-written requirements has lost half the marks. The three 'What you will do' bullets are responsibilities and must not appear as requirements — but they are not in must_not_appear because catching that is the role-profile step's job, not this one's.
